channel.title: Acme: Daily Reading List
channel.description: Noteworthy articles from across the web.

item.title: How to read a publisher royalty statement and its reserves
item.description: Cornell University Press explains the columns authors encounter on royalty statements, including sales, returns, prior balances and reserves against future returns. Particularly useful is its distinction between the reserve withheld this period and reserves from earlier periods that have now been released.

item.title: Why the 1984 Lensman anime remains trapped in rights limbo
item.description: This history traces the licensing problems behind the vanished Lensman film and television series. It reports that Harmony Gold never finalized its U.S. license, Streamline withdrew its releases after the Smith estate threatened legal action, and any revival would require negotiations whose cost may exceed the small vintage-anime market.

item.title: Copyright Office finishes digitizing 26,000 historical record books
item.description: The U.S. Copyright Office has completed digitization of more than 26,000 record books containing registrations, assignments, notices and other documents from 1870 through 1977. The images are available in a Library of Congress preview collection, with searchable metadata planned for the Copyright Public Records System.

item.title: Inside Hollywood’s surviving temple to movie books and scripts
item.description: Larry Edmunds Bookshop has served film obsessives since 1938, stocking movie histories, biographies, vintage scripts, posters and photographs. This tour of the restored neon-lit Hollywood institution is a useful companion to any search for the vanished specialty bookstores that once made screenplays easy to browse.

item.title: How SendGrid turns incoming email into an application webhook
item.description: SendGrid’s Inbound Parse feature accepts mail addressed to a configured subdomain and posts the parsed headers, text, HTML and attachments to an application URL. The walkthrough uses Rails, but the DNS and webhook pattern applies to any web stack that needs to receive email rather than merely send it.

item.title: The practical differences between iPhone 15 Pro and Pro Max
item.description: Both 2023 Pro models share the A17 Pro chip, titanium frame and USB-C, but the Max has a 6.7-inch display, longer battery life and 5x telephoto lens. The smaller Pro is lighter, uses a 6.1-inch screen and has 3x optical zoom; storage also starts at 128GB instead of 256GB.

item.title: Pep Comics archive pinpoints the Press Guardian’s public-domain run
item.description: The University of Pennsylvania’s serial archive identifies Pep Comics issues available online and notes that the first copyright-renewed issue is No. 74, dated March 1949. Paired with Grand Comics Database indexes, it provides a practical starting point for tracing Perry Chase’s Press Guardian stories through the public-domain years.

item.title: R.C. Harvey traces Bringing Up Father from Jiggs to its final strip
item.description: R.C. Harvey’s illustrated history follows George McManus from early newspaper features to Bringing Up Father, explaining the immigrant-class comedy behind Jiggs and Maggie. It fixes the strip’s debut at January 2, 1913, and records its uninterrupted run through May 28, 2000.

item.title: Jacksonville library opens a century of local newspapers to home researchers
item.description: Jacksonville Public Library expanded online access to three local newspaper archives: the Florida Times-Union from 1883 onward, the Beaches Leader from 1963, and the Jacksonville Journal from 1901 to 1988. Library cardholders can search the collections remotely.

item.title: Daniel Pinkwater’s 85th birthday invites a trip through his 500-episode archive
item.description: Daniel Pinkwater turns 85 on November 15, 2026. His official site preserves more than 500 podcast episodes made from 2007 through 2017: complete and serialized readings, unpublished stories, interviews, listener questions and assorted comic detours. It is a unusually deep free archive of a writer whose work straddles children’s books, comics, radio and eccentric speculative fiction.

item.title: A 398th Bomb Group crew page identifies Byron Hughes aboard the Black Widow
item.description: The 398th Bomb Group Memorial Association identifies 2nd Lt. Byron R. Hughes Jr. as navigator in James Mitchell’s 601st Squadron crew photo. Its notes reconstruct the January 20, 1945 loss of B-17G 43-37889, the Black Widow: flak near Mannheim, pilot Mitchell staying at the controls, and the crew’s bailout and capture.

item.title: St. Augustine’s Living History Saunter turns St. George Street into a timeline
item.description: Historic Florida Militia interpreters gather on St. George Street from 5:30 to 8:30 p.m. on November 14 for a free walk through St. Augustine’s colonial eras. Participants portray soldiers, sailors, settlers and tradespeople from the city’s Spanish and British periods, giving local history a human scale beyond museum cases and plaques.

item.title: A 1997 Washington Post review finds the Gilgamesh inside How Like a God
item.description: Joe Mayhew’s May 25, 1997 Washington Post review called Brenda W. Clough’s How Like a God “solid and even elegant.” The review reads Rob Lewis’s unwanted powers through the Gilgamesh epic and argues that the novel feels more like fantasy than conventional science fiction—a useful contemporary snapshot of the book’s reception.

item.title: FANAC preserves File 770’s December 1996 snapshot of fandom
item.description: FANAC’s File 770 archive includes issue 115 from December 1996, a 22-page scan supplied by Mark Olson. The issue offers a primary-source view of convention politics, awards, fan publishing and personalities at the end of that year—exactly the sort of searchable institutional memory that disappears when paper collections stay private.

item.title: National Archives opens a searchable trail through nine million WWII enlistment records
item.description: The National Archives explains how to search and download its electronic Army enlistment files covering 1938–1946. The database holds about nine million records, with fields such as serial number, birthplace, residence, occupation and enlistment date. Its limitations are important: it generally excludes officers and members of other service branches.
